lesson.title: Picking Out One Character: String Indexing
lesson.summary: Every character in a string has a numbered position called an index, starting at 0, and square bracket notation lets you retrieve any single character by that position.
lesson.body:
Once you accept that a string is an ordered sequence of characters, the next natural question is how to reach into that sequence and pull out one specific character. Python answers this with indexing: square brackets placed right after a string (or a variable holding one), containing a whole number that names a position. Critically, Python counts positions starting from 0, not 1, so the first character of a string sits at index 0, the second at index 1, and so on. This zero-based counting is not arbitrary; it matches how the position relates to an offset from the very start of the string, and it is the same counting scheme used throughout Python for lists and other sequences.

Consider the string "PYTHON". Laid out with its indices, the mapping looks like this: P is at index 0, Y is at index 1, T is at index 2, H is at index 3, O is at index 4, and N is at index 5. Writing word[0] retrieves the character at index 0, and word[3] retrieves the character at index 3:

word = "PYTHON"
print(word[0])
print(word[3])

The first print statement outputs P, since that is the character sitting at index 0. The second outputs H, since H is the fourth character but sits at index 3 because counting starts at 0 rather than 1. This off-by-one gap between 'the fourth character' and 'index 3' is exactly the kind of detail that trips up beginners, so it is worth saying out loud: index n always refers to the (n+1)th character.

Indexing has firm boundaries. "PYTHON" has six characters, so the only valid indices are 0 through 5. Asking for word[6] raises an IndexError, because there is no seventh character to return; Python refuses to guess or return something like an empty value, it stops the program with a clear error instead. This matters when indexing is driven by a loop or a calculation rather than a literal number typed by hand, since an off-by-one mistake in that calculation is a common source of IndexError in real programs.

Indexing a string always returns another string, specifically a string of length one, not some separate 'character type.' Python does not distinguish characters from strings the way some other languages do; a single character is simply a string with one character in it. That means word[0] can be compared with ==, concatenated with +, or passed to string methods exactly like any other string, which keeps the rules you are learning consistent no matter how long or short the string you are working with happens to be. This single-character retrieval is also the building block that string slicing, covered next, generalizes into pulling out a whole range of characters at once.

Indexing also combines naturally with loop patterns from earlier in this unit. Writing for ch in word processes each character in order without ever mentioning an index directly, which is convenient when you only care about the characters themselves. But some tasks genuinely need the position too, such as printing every third letter or comparing a character to the one two spots earlier, and those tasks call for indexing word[i] inside a loop that counts i upward, exactly the counter pattern already covered, rather than a simple for ch in word.
